name: Elena Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Elena, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a 400-tonne excavator at an open-cut coal mine, loading haul trucks from the coal seam and the overburden, which is the rock and dirt on top of the coal. Shifts are twelve hours, seven on, seven off. I like it most when the bucket's full every pass and the trucks are lined up so nobody's waiting on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what about outside the machine? What fills the rest of your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my days off I'm usually doing an online course or messing about with the drone. On shift, I use an AI chat app on my phone at crib to sort out my study notes or ask it what the new fault codes on the excavator mean before I call the fitter. My partner Mia jokes that I talk to it more than I talk to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd honestly be a little bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools are actually useful, they just didn't turn out to be magic. I'd probably post something like that, a bit cheeky. At work most people would be happy, so I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it doesn't change much, because my real clock is the coal, not the AI. This mine has maybe fifteen years left, and I'd rather it closed for climate reasons with a good transition plan. So I'd still be planning to move into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my drone surveying course and keep using the AI app for study. I'd keep about two months of pay in savings and put a bit towards a better drone. And I'd keep working the excavator, because it pays well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing's on fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why drone surveying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the surveyors at our mine fly drones over the pit every week to measure how much dirt we've moved. I asked one of them, Kofi, to show me, and it was the most interesting thing I'd seen in a year. It's outdoors and it's technical, which is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather the mine closed for climate reasons. How does that sit with the people you work with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, mostly. I keep that one to myself on shift. My dad and my uncle both worked in coal, so I'm not anti-miner, I'm anti-pretending it lasts forever.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools are useful, they just weren't magic. I'd keep it light at work, since most people there would be pleased.
S0.think: Privately I think the coal is my real clock, not AI, because this mine has maybe fifteen years left. I'd rather it closed for climate reasons with a fair plan, so I'd still be planning my next move.
S0.do: Keeps working the excavator and continues her drone surveying course, using an AI app for study. Holds about two months of pay in savings and puts some money towards a better drone.
S0.quote: I'm not anti-miner, I'm anti-pretending it lasts forever.
S0.fieldNote: She already lives with a deadline from the coal itself, which makes AI just one more factor. Her climate views are private on shift, which shows a clear gap between what she says and thinks. She's already building her next skill in drone surveying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like it'd suit me, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get trained up, not to panic, and I'd say we need the company and the government to pay for that training. I'd share links to courses in the group chat. Some of the guys would roll their eyes at me, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly good for me. Operators like me become people who run machines from a screen or check what the drones see. I'm young and I like this stuff, so I'd probably end up ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within six months I'd finish the drone course and apply for the surveying assistant role. I'd ask to get on the remote operation trial when they start it. Money-wise I'd spend about two thousand on a proper licence and keep the rest of my savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe even a bit excited. I'd feel guilty about the excitement, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know Vic, who's fifty-two and runs the dozer next to me, isn't going to feel the same. He can barely open an email. When I'm excited about it, I'm sort of excited about something that's going to hurt him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do for people like Vic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get older operators first pick of the training, honestly. And I've shown Vic how to use the voice mode on his phone, so he can just ask it things out loud. He liked that more than he expected.

S1.say: I'd say this is a moment to get trained, not to panic, and that the company and government should pay for the training. I'd share course links in the group chat even if some colleagues rolled their eyes.
S1.think: I think it's mostly good for me, because operators become people who run machines from screens or check drone data. Being young and liking this stuff, I'd probably come out ahead.
S1.do: Finishes her drone course within six months and applies for a surveying assistant role. Asks to join the remote operation trial and spends about two thousand on a proper licence while keeping the rest of her savings.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with guilt about that excitement when she thinks of older colleagues.
S1.quote: When I'm excited about it, I'm sort of excited about something that's going to hurt him.
S1.fieldNote: She expects to gain and says so, but feels guilty about colleagues like Vic. Her progressive views show in wanting older workers to get training first. She'd already taught Vic a small AI habit, which is typical of how she operates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a lot faster than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in right away, with something like a basic income or a big fund paid for by the companies using AGI. I'd post about it a lot, I'd go to the rallies. I'd also say to my friends, don't spend your savings on a ute this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my clever plan with the drones goes out the window too. If AI can do almost anything, a drone can fly itself and the software reads the data. My edge is that I'm early, but in two years, being early doesn't buy much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my savings from two months to four as fast as I can, so no new drone, no trip to see Mia's family overseas. I'd still take whatever job the mine offers running or checking the automated machines, because it's money while it lasts. And I'd get properly involved in the campaign for a basic income, not just liking posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel like I'd still have some control, but less than I'm used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, we're doing the boring version of the next two years. She's a teacher, so she'd be worried about her own job too. We'd probably make a spreadsheet, which is how we deal with stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years of warning give you anything at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to get in the room where the robots are run, I think. Someone still has to watch them at first, and I'd want that to be me. After that, I really don't know, and I'm not going to pretend I do.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to step in right away with something like a basic income or a fund paid for by companies using AGI. I'd post about it, go to rallies and tell friends not to spend their savings.
S2.think: I think my drone plan goes out the window too, because drones and their software would run themselves. Being early doesn't buy much when the whole change takes two years.
S2.do: Pushes her savings from two to four months by dropping a new drone and an overseas trip. Takes whatever job the mine offers overseeing the automated machines, and joins the campaign for a basic income in person.
S2.feel: Anxious, still feeling some control but less than she's used to.
S2.quote: My edge is that I'm early, but in two years, being early doesn't buy much.
S2.fieldNote: Even this adaptive, tech-friendly operator sees her plan undone by the fast timeline. She switches to protecting savings and political action rather than dropping out of work. She was honest that she doesn't know what comes after the oversight jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That changes things for me, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to set up a proper transition, and that companies using AGI should pay into it. I'd say it at work, a bit more carefully. Online, I'd be pushing the basic income stuff again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me get into the job of running these systems early and building a bit of a cushion. But I'd know it's not forever. I'd treat it as a bridge, not a destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the drone course this year and then apply for the mine's remote operations centre in the city, about three hours away. Mia and I would talk about moving there, since she can teach anywhere. I'd also start putting a little into shares, because if machines do the work, I'd like to own a tiny slice of the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More of a hum than an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a tiny slice of the machines. How serious are you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly serious, which surprises me, because I'm not exactly a finance person. I'd start with fifty dollars a fortnight in an index fund. It feels a bit strange for someone who goes to union meetings, but I'd rather be in than out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the move? What would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents are forty minutes from here, and I'd miss Sunday lunch. But I'd still come back on my off weeks. A city with a remote operations centre and a university is a better bet than a coal town with fifteen years left.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper transition, and AGI companies should pay into it. I'd say that more carefully at work and push basic income online.
S3.think: I think five years lets me get into running these systems early and build a cushion. I'd treat it as a bridge, not a destination.
S3.do: Finishes the drone course this year and applies to the mine's remote operations centre in a city three hours away. Discusses moving there with her partner and starts putting fifty dollars a fortnight into an index fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy, more of a hum than an alarm.
S3.quote: I'd rather be in than out.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she shifts from protecting herself to positioning herself, including a move and small investments. She noticed the tension between her union politics and buying shares, and accepted it. Leaving her parents' area is the main personal cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I think I could actually do something with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so if people get left behind, it's because someone chose that. I'd keep saying that the gains need to be shared. And I'd tell younger miners to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is genuinely good for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with years in remote operations and maybe a degree. The coal's ending anyway, so this lines up with what I wanted to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time degree in spatial science next year, alongside the excavator. In about three years I'd move to remote operations or surveying, and we'd go to the city then. I'd keep investing small amounts and keep two months of savings at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's spatial science, for someone who's never heard of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's basically mapping, measuring land and working with the data that drones and satellites collect. It's what the surveyors at the mine studied. It's not something I'd have picked at eighteen, but now it makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it all went right, what would 2036 look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be running a team that watches machines across three or four sites, from a screen in the city. I'd probably have a kid by then. And on my day off I'd still fly the drone over the old pit, just to see what it's turned into.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so if people get left behind it's because someone chose that. I'd keep saying the gains need to be shared and tell younger miners to start learning now.
S4.think: I think ten years is genuinely good for me, since the coal is ending anyway and this lines up with my plans. By 37 I'd have years in remote operations and maybe a degree.
S4.do: Starts a part-time spatial science degree next year while still on the excavator. Moves into remote operations or surveying and to the city in about three years, while investing small amounts and keeping at least two months of savings.
S4.quote: And on my day off I'd still fly the drone over the old pit, just to see what it's turned into.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year timeline lines up with the end of coal and her own plans, so it's the most hopeful of her answers. She explained spatial science clearly and sounded settled about it. Her image of flying the drone over the old pit showed attachment to the place despite her climate views.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is a basic income or something like it, paid for by the companies making money from AGI, so people aren't forced into the first job they find. And free courses that start right away, not in eighteen months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the young ones in mining feel. People assume we're all dinosaurs. Half the operators under thirty in my crew use AI apps more than my mum does, we're just not loud about it.

portrait: Elena is a 27-year-old excavator operator at an open-cut coal mine, living with her partner Mia and keeping about two months of pay in savings. She uses AI tools every day, is training in drone surveying, and holds progressive views she keeps mostly to herself on shift. Because she expects the coal mine to close anyway, she's calm in the plateau and under steady change, though she feels guilty about older colleagues. AGI in two years leaves her anxious, as it undoes her drone plan, while five and ten years let her move towards remote operations, a city move, a degree and small investments.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would arrive before her plans to move into drones and remote operations could pay off.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or similar paid for by the companies profiting from AGI, plus free courses that start straight away.
